title: Don’t Cast Team Obligations as Goals During the Review and Planning Process
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This piece warns leaders against a common goal-setting mistake: treating everyday responsibilities that team members already owe the organization — like giving honest feedback, meeting deadlines, or sharing information — as aspirational goals rather than baseline obligations. Doing so, the author argues, signals that these behaviors are optional and erodes accountability for being a productive team member. Instead, when someone is falling short of a basic standard, leaders should address it directly as a performance expectation to meet now, not frame it as a year-long goal to work toward. The article closes by urging leaders to audit their planning conversations for this distinction before finalizing next year's goals.
points: A common goal-setting error is classifying everyday team-member obligations — feedback, deadlines, information-sharing — as aspirational goals.
This framing signals that basic responsibilities are optional, undermining accountability for being a good team member.
When someone underperforms on a baseline expectation, leaders should address it as a standard to meet now, not a year-long goal.
Leaders should audit whether their planning conversations conflate obligations with goals before finalizing plans.
quotes: One of the most common errors leaders make in the goal-setting process is to classify everyday obligations and commitments as goals to achieve rather than as responsibilities to uphold
Casting everyday responsibilities as goals reduces accountability for being a productive team member.
It sends the message that the obligations and commitments of being a team member are optional or elective.
This pass-or-fail mentality sets the standard for all team members.
In that case, have the discussion to meet the standard, but don’t present them as goals. A great team culture depends on it.
